newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Crucial RBNZ independence preserved - economists.
newsitem.headline: Crucial RBNZ independence preserved - economists.

text.p: A coalition deal between the National and New Zealand First parties appears to preserve the Reserve Bank's operational independence and financial markets can live with it, analysts said on Tuesday.
Nationalist NZ First, which held the balance of power, brought two months of suspense to an end when it chose the conservative National Party in preference to centre-left Labour.
A few hearts fluttered initially when it was announced the goal of "sustainable economic growth" would be added to the RBNZ's Policy Targets Agreement (PTA) with the government.
However, the Reserve Bank Act itself, which defines price stability as the bank's sole objective, was left intact.

Economists said that would help neutralise the PTA's growth goal. "In no way can the PTA, the goal of that, be inconsistent with price stability, which is the Reserve Bank Act," said National Bank Chief Economist Adrian Orr.

"Independence remains firmly installed there...(RBNZ Governor Don) Brash will happily tell the world that the best way of (achieving) sustained growth is through price stability. I think they've got themselves very well legally covered in terms of the Reserve Bank Act and Policy Targets Agreement."
Brash, who has been outspoken against widening the RBNZ's objectives to include economic growth, said he was happy to work with the new PTA.
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said the inclusion of sustainable economic growth in the PTA didn't seem on the face of it to be a substantive change.
Economists agreed a widening of the RBNZ's target band for annual underlying inflation to 0-3 percent from the current 0-2 percent had been well flagged.

"I don't agree with the change but I think 0-3 is something we can live with. But it will raise questions about whether they change it (the target band) again once inflation gets above three percent. There's no doubt it will," Plank said.
He said the fiscal policy stance for 1997 did not seem to deviate greatly from previous projections, although increased social spending in place of further income tax cuts would be more inflationary.
The delay by a year of the government's second round of tax cuts, which had been due to come into effect on July 1, 1997, had also been well signposted.
Orr saw the "inevitable" rise in government spending and the deferred tax cuts cancelling each other out.
"It certainly looks like spending next year will have more or less the same impact on inflation as the tax cuts would have done anyway over that 12-month period," he said.
The economists said that by raising the mid-point of the inflation target band to 1.5 percent, the path had been paved for lower interest rates.
"There is potential for rates to go lower in this particular easing cycle than I think the market had previously anticipated," said Chris Rand, Westpac's chief manager of forex and money markets.

Westpac economists thought short-term rates could drop to just below eight percent from their current 8.42 percent, but the futures market (the only money market open for trade on Tuesday night) had gone further and was indicating rates closer to seven percent by March, Rand said.
National Bank's Orr said the coalition announcement should not greatly affect the RBNZ's monetary policy statement on December 17, in which the market expects a monetary easing.
"In terms of upsetting the Reserve Bank's plans with regard to the monetary policy statement in a few days, it shouldn't widely throw them off the mark," Orr said.
